rv.q: It's pleasingly experimental, but not all ideas coalesce in Jeff James's production, in which a combination of fourth-wall breaking and direct address sees the boundaries blur further.
What remains is something bold and confident, but lost in a miasma of tricksy dialogue and didactic passion.
Whilst there is lots to like, sadly the whole never quite lives up to the sum of its parts, thus making this a disappointing end to this year’s Minerva season at Chichester.
I implore all who can to take a chance on this remarkable play, as it is an hour and 15 minutes worth of theatre that will stay with you for a long time after.
Nina Segal’s bold and powerful adaptation of the ancient Greek tragedy should prove to be as classic as the original!
In summary this was an intriguing, and thought-provoking addition to the Antigone myth which does not outstay its welcome, albeit not always successfully contemporising its mythical origins.
All in all it was a thought-provoking and often uncomfortable watch that examined universal themes under a modern lens.
A fine premiss, a gifted playwright with a superb, hard-working cast seems slightly adrift; but still addressing themes that frankly most other playwrights don’t dare to touch.

As a 21st century interpretation of both a Greek classic and experimental theatre, this is an interesting technical experience, well performed, a little preachy at times but certainly prompts debate and reflection on the way home which we are sure is the intent.
Its ancient questions remain, but the ways in which they are asked make this a thought-provoking and often deeply moving piece of theatre.
It’s a powerful one-act play that tells the story of Antigone with great clarity and attempts to put a relevant spin on it for a modern audience.

cn.t: An experimental Greek tragedy reworking divides critics: some praise its innovation and emotional power, while others find the modern updates heavy-handed and the fourth-wall breaking production gimmicky.
